_comment: agent 站 52 份档案的正文首段（panel-lead）英文。2026-10-04 建；2026-10-08 A6.1 扩至 52 份。
_note: 这些内容与 _onelines.en.json 的定位句高度重合（同一批作者写的位置说明），但用词更完整 —— 有的带官方引用与安全警告。**保留原文的强调与立场**：
_rules: 0) 保留 ** 强调（那是作者标注的「关键差别在哪」）。
1) 保留官方引用块的原文（英文引用不译，直接引）。
2) 保留安全警告的强度（明确标注 can reach local and internal IPs 这类不能软化）。
3) 产品名 / 参数 / 文档名原样（Aider in your IDE、npx、ACP、Atom feed）。
aider-cli: A terminal pair-programming tool where **Git integration is core design, not an add-on** — AI changes always live in version control, diffable and revertible.
aider: **Not an editor plugin but a usage mode** — Aider stays resident and watches your files; add an AI comment in any editor and it responds.
claude-code-cli: **The highest data quality and most frequent releases in this track** — it ships its own CHANGELOG and Atom feed, with the finest granularity in permission design.
claude-code: **One process, three entry points** — terminal, IDE and GitHub `@claude` mentions all share the same permission and context mechanism.
cline: **The only object here covering all three forms** — CLI, desktop app and VS Code extension share one open-source core, and the model is selectable.
codex-cli: OpenAI's official terminal coding agent, **written in Rust**, architecturally centred on the app server and thread resumption.
codex-ide: **Not a standalone IDE but an extension for VS Code / Cursor / Windsurf** — sharing the same session mechanism with the CLI through the app server.
copilot: **The widest form coverage and the most GitHub-bound ecosystem** — website, CLI and mainstream editors, and it can delegate tasks to Claude / Codex (Preview).
crush: A TUI coding agent in the Charm ecosystem, with **the most complete annotation of the three MCP transports**, plus an official subscription plan, Hyper.
cursor: **One of the three most architecturally aggressive here**: a cloud agent that keeps running when you close the laptop, self-hosted code that never leaves the network, and code review split across two bots.
gemini-cli: Google's official open-source terminal agent — **no install via npx, explicit MCP support, and a non-interactive script mode**; the most complete engineering of the three.
grok-bot: **Of the three released at the same time, the only one whose official page lists the jobs** — it does not discuss mechanism, it lists nine roles directly (sales leads, site building, inbox triage, meeting attendance and more).
meta-muse: **The only one that hands approval authority to another agent** — two system-isolated things run on the Muse Secure VM: Muse doing the work, and Sentinel able to veto it.
openai-dot: **Nothing installs locally; all work happens on OpenAI's cloud machine** — the stated capability boundary is blunt: a standalone cloud computer plus its own browser plus plugins into 4,000+ apps, and it keeps progressing after you shut down.
opencode: An MIT-licensed multi-provider programming harness that **asks permission before running bash commands**, and supports loading via ACP.
windsurf: **Now renamed Devin Desktop** (after the Cognition acquisition) — it has its own SWE-2 model, supports ACP preview, and has a CVE fix history involving Restricted Mode.
zed: **Not "yet another AI coding tool" but an orchestration layer for three agent paths** — use Zed's native agent in the same editor, or attach Claude / Codex / OpenCode / Copilot / Cursor.
claude-agent-sdk: **"The programming interface to Claude Code"** — not a framework for building your own agent, but a mature coding CLI turned into an object you can drive from Python.
codex-sdk:
**"Turns the Codex CLI into an object you can drive inside a Node process"** — the official README opens with "Embed the Codex agent in your workflows and apps"; the second sentence settles the form:

> The TypeScript SDK **wraps** the `codex` CLI from `@openai/codex`.
> It **spawns the CLI** and exchanges JSONL events over stdin/stdout.
crewai:
**"Organises multi-agent collaboration through role division and business process"** — the official description reads:

> Framework for orchestrating **role-playing**, autonomous AI agents.

**The word "role-playing" makes people underrate it** — the same README also says production-grade and promises to "move from experiment to production **without changing frameworks**".
deepagents: **"A batteries-included agent harness"** — described officially as ready to run out of the box and aimed at long, multi-step tasks.
google-adk:
**"A code-first agent orchestration framework whose core asset is a graph execution engine"** — the first feature listed in the official README states its identity:

> **Workflow Runtime**: A graph-based execution engine for composing **deterministic
> execution flows** for agentic apps, with support for routing, fan-out/fan-in,
> **loops**, **retry**, **state management**, **dynamic nodes**, **human-in-the-loop**,
> and **nested workflows**.
hermes-agent:
**"The only resident personal assistant with a learning loop"** — the official README puts it this way:

> **The self-improving AI agent** built by Nous Research.
> It's the only agent with a **built-in learning loop** — it creates skills from experience,
> improves them during use, **nudges itself to persist knowledge**, searches its own past
> conversations, and builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions.
> Run it on a $5 VPS, a GPU cluster, or serverless infrastructure that costs nearly nothing when idle.
> **It's not tied to your laptop** — talk to it from Telegram while it works on a cloud VM.

⚠ **This site's position on "the only agent"**: that is the **vendor's own marketing line**. This site **ran no cross-product comparison to verify that "only" holds**. It is recorded as a vendor claim, not as this site's conclusion.
langgraph:
**"A low-level orchestration framework"** — the official description is deliberately modest; note that word, low-level:

> Low-level orchestration framework for building **stateful** agents.

It does not claim to be a batteries-included high-level wrapper, but the infrastructure underneath long-running, stateful work.
llamaindex:
**⚠ But one thing has to be stated first: the project has explicitly moved its company focus away from "orchestration frameworks".**

The NOTE block at the top of the README reads (checked 2026-10-01):

> The **current focus** of LlamaIndex is to build the best AI-powered engine for
> **document parsing and extraction**. **LlamaParse** is our **enterprise platform** for
> agentic OCR, parsing, extraction, indexing and more.
> >
> ...the company itself has undergone an **evolution** since when this OSS framework
> first launched 3 years ago in 2023.
> >
> While we still have the OSS framework available as an open toolkit that you're welcome
> to use, **our primary focus has shifted towards LlamaParse**...

**The selection implication is direct**: if what you want is multi-agent orchestration / workflows, **that capability now lives in the commercial platform LlamaAgents** — the README puts Workflows in the commercial platform section (the link points at `cloud/llamaagents`), not the OSS section.

**What the OSS framework now really provides**: data ingestion + indices/graph structures + retrieval query interfaces + 300+ integrations. The README's own "Proposed Solution" list puts it precisely:

> - **data connectors** to ingest your existing data sources and data formats (APIs, PDFs, docs, SQL, etc.)
> - ways to **structure your data** (indices, graphs)
> - an **advanced retrieval/query interface** over your data
> - easy **integrations with your outer application framework**

**This site's inclusion judgement**: it meets the v3 inclusion criteria (pushed 2026-09-29, still active), but the real value of this entry is **recording that turn honestly** — so readers know that behind those 52,377★ the company is heading towards document parsing / agentic OCR, which is LlamaParse and ParseBench territory, not this open-source framework's.
openai-agents-sdk: **"A primitives-only multi-agent harness"** — the official description is "lightweight yet powerful": it hands you the agent-loop primitives and does not decide for you how the filesystem, planning or memory work.
openhands:
**"A self-hosted control centre for agents"** — the official README now calls it **Agent Canvas**, with the positioning stated as:

> The self-hosted developer control center for coding agents and automations.
> Run OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or **any ACP-compatible agent**
> across local, remote, and cloud backends.
context7: **The only remotely hosted entry in the MCP track** — version-aware library documentation for agents; MIT-licensed, but the core service lives on Upstash's side.
everything: **Not a usable tool** — the official page states plainly that this server exists for MCP client developers to run functional tests against; its only purpose is verifying that a client implements the protocol correctly.
fetch: A reference server that converts web pages to Markdown, **with an explicit security warning in its official README: it can reach local and internal IPs**.
filesystem: The file-operation implementation among MCP's official reference servers, **requiring allowed directories to be declared explicitly, with no silent whole-disk access**.
git: The version-control implementation among MCP's official reference servers, **scoped to a given git repository but with full local write capability**.
memory: A reference server implementing cross-session persistent memory with a local knowledge graph — **memory is written to disk, shared across sessions, with no access control**.
playwright: A browser automation server maintained by Microsoft, **driven by the accessibility tree rather than screenshots** — no vision model needed, and the output is a structured snapshot.
sequential-thinking: Provides a single `sequential_thinking` tool that lets an agent work through a complex problem **in a revisable, branchable way** — **it produces no intelligence, only structure**.
time: Does two things only: report the current time and convert time zones. **No files, no network — the lowest-risk category of server.**
ag2: AG2 is an open-source Python framework for building AI agents and coordinating multiple agents to solve tasks, offering "agents capable of interacting with each other," broad LLM support, tooling, autonomous and human-in-the-loop workflows, and multi-agent conversation patterns. It is the community continuation of AutoGen: as of **v1.0** the protocol-driven framework became the top-level package (`import ag2`), while the classic framework (`ConversableAgent`, `GroupChat`, `import autogen`) moved to its own repository, `ag2ai/ag2-classic`. Officially, "AG2 v1.0 (`pip install ag2`) is **not** a drop-in upgrade from Classic. The agent model, orchestration, and imports all changed." v1.0 orchestrates agents through the **Network** — a `Hub` that owns the registry, write-ahead log, and audit trail, with agents talking over typed **channels** (`conversation` / `consulting` / `discussion` / `workflow`) — and exposes an opt-in **harness** of composable primitives (`assembly=`, `knowledge=`, `tasks=`). It is licensed Apache-2.0 and runs entirely in your own process (no managed hosting).
amp:
Official positioning: "Amp is the frontier agent and development environment that lets you build from anywhere."

**The signature feature is the orb** — "Machines that Amp creates per thread, with your code, tools, and plugins already set up. Send a prompt, close your laptop, and the agent keeps working." Threads can run locally, in an **orb** (a machine Amp creates in the cloud) or on one of your own **runners** (`--executor local|orb|runner:<id>`). Architecturally Amp is two components: the local **Amp Client** (primarily the CLI — local code/context, settings and thread history) and the **Amp Server** at ampcode.com (a multi-tenant service on Google Cloud Platform handling auth, thread sync and LLM proxying).

Amp is multi-model and routes by task: the four agent modes (`low` / `medium` / `high` / `ultra`) are officially described as "capability presets, not fixed model selectors", with the `oracle` tool offering a stronger second-opinion model. Pricing starts free: "Start free. Scale your orbs and team."
continue:
**An open-source, fully model-configurable IDE extension** — VS Code extension, JetBrains plugin and a `cn` CLI over one agent core, with models configured freely in `config.yaml`. The official model-provider list spans Anthropic, Azure AI Foundry, Amazon Bedrock, DeepSeek, Gemini, Mistral, **Ollama (local models)**, OpenAI, Vertex AI, xAI and "More (30 items)".

**But the official status has changed.** The homepage now reads "Continue has been acquired by Cursor... our open-source codebase remains freely available as a foundation for others", and the repository README states: "The `continuedev/continue` repository is no longer actively maintained and is read-only for all users." The last releases are the final 2.0.0 line for the VS Code extension, CLI and JetBrains plugin (Apache-2.0 © 2023-2026 Continue Dev, Inc.). The commercial line's pricing page (hub.continue.dev/pricing) now serves **Continuous AI**: Starter $3 / million tokens pay-as-you-go, Team $20 / seat / month (including $10 in credits per seat), Company custom.
copilot-cli: The same product as this site's GitHub Copilot IDE entry, in a different form factor: a terminal agent that also has a programmatic mode (`copilot -p`) and per-tool approval flags. What changes here is the billing unit and the approval surface. Billing: "Each time you submit a prompt to Copilot CLI, your monthly quota of Copilot premium requests is reduced by one," and "Each prompt to Copilot CLI uses one premium request with the default model. For other models, this is multiplied by the model's rate." Approval: the first time a file-modifying or executing tool is requested, the CLI offers three choices — "1. Yes / 2. Yes, and approve TOOL for the rest of the running session / 3. No, and tell Copilot what to do differently (Esc)" — and headless runs use `--allow-all-tools` / `--allow-tool` / `--deny-tool`, where deny wins.
cursor-cli:
**The terminal form of Cursor, sharing one account, model catalogue and `mcp.json` with the editor.** The official CLI changelog treats it as its own product line (separate from IDE / Agents Window / SDK), and the docs describe headless use as "print mode (`-p, --print`) for non-interactive scripting and automation".

The command is `agent` (installed under `~/.local/bin`), and beyond plain terminal work it adds two paths the IDE form does not have: handing a conversation to a **Cloud Agent** by prepending `&` to a message, and **persistent sessions** (`agent persist`, detaching with `/detach`) that, in the official wording, "keep agents running after you disconnect". Permission tokens (`Shell` / `Read` / `Write` / `WebFetch` / `Mcp`) are enforced from `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` or a project-level `.cursor/cli.json`, with deny taking precedence over allow.
factory-droid: Factory AI's terminal coding agent. Its pitch is **model independence** — the official BYOK page says "Use your own OpenAI or Anthropic keys, connect to any open source model providers, or run models locally", and **your keys stay local: "Your API keys remain local and are not uploaded to Factory servers"**. Quota is not one monthly bucket but three independent rolling windows (5-hour / 7-day / 30-day); when you hit one you can fall back to **Droid Core** (a free open-weight model pool) or **Extra Usage** (prepaid credits, $10 minimum, never expiring). Every mutating action is gated by an **Autonomy Level** (Off / Low / Medium / High) plus command allow / deny / block lists. And it is not a single CLI: the official pricing page lists the Pro tier as "Factory App / Droid CLI / Droid SDK".
github-mcp:
GitHub's official MCP server (repository description: "GitHub's official MCP Server"). It connects any MCP client to GitHub's platform: reading repositories and code files, managing issues and PRs, monitoring Actions, inspecting code-scanning / Dependabot findings, and reading notifications.

**Two forms.** The **remote hosted** server (`https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, Streamable HTTP) is "hosted by GitHub and provides the easiest method for getting up and running... no local setup or runtime required." The **local** server runs as an stdio process via Docker (`ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server`) or a Go binary; GitHub Enterprise Server is only supported locally.

**Toolsets are the headline mechanism**: enable only what you need to help the LLM pick tools and shrink context. Default toolsets are `context, repos, issues, pull_requests, users`; 20+ groups exist in total, and the remote server adds extras (Copilot Spaces, Support Docs Search, `create_pull_request_with_copilot`).

**Two caution notes.** read-only mode is a "strict security filter" that takes precedence over everything else (write tools are skipped even if explicitly requested). Lockdown mode is explicitly "a best-effort content filter... **not** an authorization boundary."

Auth is OAuth (with scope challenges on the remote server) or a PAT (classic PATs get startup scope filtering; fine-grained PATs are not filtered). MIT licensed. Repository metadata (checked 2026-10-08): 33,446★, Go, latest release v2.0.2.
goose:
A general-purpose AI agent that runs on your machine, not just for code — official README: "goose is a general-purpose AI agent that runs on your machine. Not just for code — use it for research, writing, automation, data analysis, or anything you need to get done."

**Three forms, local first**: "A native desktop app for macOS, Linux, and Windows. A full CLI for terminal workflows. An API to embed it anywhere. Built in Rust for performance and portability." It works with 15+ providers — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, **Ollama**, OpenRouter, Azure, Bedrock and more — using API keys, local models, or your existing Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini subscriptions via ACP, and connects to 70+ extensions through the Model Context Protocol.

**Stewardship note (checked 2026-10-08)**: Block donated goose to the **Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)** at the Linux Foundation (official blog, 2026-04-07); the repository now redirects to `aaif-goose/goose` and the README states goose is part of AAIF. This entry records `vendor: Agentic AI Foundation` as the current steward — matching this site's convention of recording the current owner (as with Windsurf → Cognition) — while Block is the creator and remains credited in the body; `homepage` points at the current canonical repository. The documentation site has also moved to `goose-docs.ai` (old links redirect).
jules: Google's asynchronous coding agent: point it at a GitHub repo, and it clones the code into a fresh cloud VM, plans the change, and opens a pull request for review. The difference from the IDE/CLI agents on this site is that the interaction is not live — you approve the plan and walk away. The official REST docs make the default explicit: "By default, sessions created through the API will have their plans automatically approved. If you want to create a session that requires explicit plan approval, set the `requirePlanApproval` field to `true`"; and "The `automationMode` field is optional. By default, no PR will be automatically created." Tiers are bundled, not sold separately: the GA post describes a free "Introductory access to Jules," "Jules in Google AI Pro: 5x higher limits" and "Jules in Google AI Ultra: 20x higher limits," noting that "Specific usage limits are listed at jules.google."
junie: Junie is JetBrains' coding agent, installed as a plugin — the official install page states "The Junie plugin is not bundled and not enabled in JetBrains IDEs by default" — and extended in March 2026 by a standalone Junie CLI for the terminal, any IDE, CI/CD and GitHub / GitLab. Its official framing is LLM-agnostic: "Junie supports all the top-performing models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Grok." On the IDE side it plans before it codes and, since GA, drives your IDE's real debugger rather than adding `println`.
kiro: Kiro is a desktop IDE — officially "a desktop development environment built on a VS Code foundation" — but it is framed as one agent, every surface: the IDE, CLI, Web and Mobile apps are all front ends to the same unified agent harness, connected over the open Agent Client Protocol (ACP). Its headline workflow is spec-driven development, turning a prompt into "requirements, architectural designs, and sequenced tasks", and its cloud sandbox sessions keep working "whether or not you're connected".
mastra:
A framework for building AI-powered applications and agents on a modern TypeScript stack. Official highlights: **model routing** ("Connect to 40+ providers through one standard interface", while the `/models` directory page states "7815 models from 213 providers through a single API"), **agents**, a **graph-based workflow engine** using an explicit control-flow syntax (`.then()`, `.branch()`, `.parallel()`), **human-in-the-loop** via suspend/resume, **memory**, **RAG**, **MCP servers**, plus built-in **evals** and observability.

**State across restarts is first-class**: "Suspension saves the current execution state as a snapshot ... stored in your configured storage provider and persist across deployments and application restarts." **Local models are officially supported** through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with LMStudio recommended (`id: "lmstudio/..."`, `url: "http://localhost:1234/v1"`).

**Licensing is dual** (checked 2026-10-08): the core framework is **Apache-2.0**, while code under any `ee/` directory is **source-available under the Mastra Enterprise License** (the repo license API returns NOASSERTION). A separate commercial **Mastra platform** (Observability / Studio / Server) is priced Starter $0, Teams $250/month, Enterprise custom — Studio, hosted observability, and deployment are platform products, not part of the open-source framework. Latest `@mastra/core` is 1.75.0 (2026-10-07); requires Node.js >= 22.13.0.
microsoft-agent-framework: Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) is an open, multi-language framework from Microsoft for building **production-grade AI agents and multi-agent workflows** in **.NET and Python**. The official overview page describes it as the direct successor of two Microsoft lines: "It brings together and extends ideas from **Semantic Kernel and AutoGen** projects... Built by the same teams, it is the **unified foundation** for building AI agents going forward." It offers two primary API categories — **AI agents** (individual agents that call tools and MCP servers) and **Workflows** (graph-based workflows that drive multi-agent orchestration, with type-based routing, nesting, **checkpointing**, and request/response patterns for human-in-the-loop). Workflows execute in **supersteps** and checkpoint after each one, with three swappable storage backends (InMemory, File, Azure Cosmos DB). MAF is built around open standards — **MCP, A2A, and OpenAPI** — and ships checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, OpenTelemetry observability, middleware, declarative YAML agents, and a DevUI. It is licensed MIT and is currently in **public preview**.
pydantic-ai:
A Python agent framework that brings "the FastAPI feeling" to GenAI app and agent development, built by the Pydantic team. Official overview: "**Model-agnostic**: Supports **virtually every** model and provider" — from OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, Groq, Mistral and xAI to AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud, Azure AI Foundry, and local/self-hosted paths like **Ollama**, vLLM and LiteLLM, selected with a `<provider>:<model>` string (e.g. `Agent('openai:gpt-5.2')`).

**Two differentiators set it apart from the OpenAI Agents SDK**, the other thin Python agent-loop library. First, **type safety end to end**: structured output, typed dependency injection, and typed tools are all Pydantic-native. Second, **durable execution with eight officially supported engines** — Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate, AWS Lambda, Kitaru, Airflow and Absurd — where "each engine wraps **every model request and tool call as its own durable unit**", so a run "survives restarts, failures, and long waits". Note the official boundary: "**Durability is not storage**" — a durable engine keeps one run alive; storing chat threads is a separate concern (`Persistence`).

It also ships **Pydantic AI Harness** (memory, guardrails, sub-agents, planning, context compaction, persistence as composable `capabilities`, plus complete Coder/Researcher agents) and the standalone **`pydantic-graph`** typed state machine. License MIT; latest release v2.54.0 (2026-10-02). Commercial add-ons (Pydantic Logfire observability, Pydantic AI Gateway) are optional, and the library is "always has been, always will be ... completely free and permissively licensed under the MIT license".
smolagents:
A thin agent library from Hugging Face. The repository description is literal: "smolagents: a **barebones library for agents that think in code**."

**The core difference is code-as-action.** The default `CodeAgent` "works mostly like classical ReAct agents - the exception being that the LLM engine writes its actions as Python code snippets" (README). The official claim is that this "uses **30% fewer steps**" and "reaches higher performance on difficult benchmarks" than JSON tool calling. A conventional `ToolCallingAgent` (structured JSON) is also provided "for scenarios where that paradigm is preferred."

**Model-agnostic by design**: `InferenceClientModel` (HF Inference Providers — Cerebras, Cohere, Together, Replicate, SambaNova and more), `LiteLLMModel` ("100+ different models", incl. OpenAI / Anthropic), `OpenAIModel` (OpenAI-compatible endpoints), `AzureOpenAIModel`, `AmazonBedrockModel`, and local `TransformersModel` / `MLXModel` / Ollama. Swapping providers means swapping a Model class.

**On safety the docs are blunt**: the built-in `LocalPythonExecutor` "is **not** a security sandbox. It applies some restrictions but can be bypassed and must not be used as a security boundary." Real isolation requires a remote sandbox — Blaxel, E2B, Modal or Docker.

Repository metadata (checked 2026-10-08): 29,693★, Apache-2.0, latest release 1.26.0 (2026-05-29), Python 3.10+.
warp: Warp calls itself, verbatim, an open-source **Agentic Development Environment** that "brings together terminal work, coding agents, and cloud automation". The same **Warp Agent** is reachable three ways — "In the Warp app", "In any terminal, with the Warp Agent CLI", "In the cloud, as a cloud agent" — with account, rules, skills and model access shared across all three. The CLI is "a standalone terminal program" and "a native terminal multiplexer" with its own PTY, so it runs in any terminal emulator, **including over SSH**. Every proposed action is checked against an execution profile whose values are `agent_decides` / `always_ask` / `always_allow`; file edits still prompt every time by default, so "you always review a diff before it's applied".
